blocks.prompt: The Log That Was Not a Log
blocks.text: A crocodile can float so still that it looks like an old log. Its eyes and its nose sit on top of its head. That way it can see and breathe while the rest of it hides under the water. A crocodile has huge muscles for shutting its mouth. It has small, weak muscles for opening it. Its tail is thick and heavy. The tail is what makes it fast in the water. The mom crocodile digs a nest and lays her eggs. When her babies are ready, they chirp from inside the shells. She hears them. She digs them out and carries them to the water in her mouth.

blocks.prompt: The Log That Watches
blocks.text: A crocodile spends most of its day doing almost nothing. It floats near the edge of a river with only its eyes and nostrils above the surface. The rest of its body hangs below, hidden in the brown water. From the bank it looks like a floating log. That stillness is the whole plan. A crocodile does not chase its food across the water. It waits for its food to walk to the river. When something comes close enough, the crocodile lunges in less than a second. Its jaws slam shut with more force than any other living animal can manage. Here is the strange part. The muscles that close a crocodile's mouth are enormous. The muscles that open it again are small and weak. A grown person could hold those jaws shut with two hands. Nobody should try, because the closing is the part that matters. A crocodile cannot chew. It has no flat teeth for grinding, only sharp ones for gripping. So it holds on, spins its whole body in a roll, and tears off a piece to swallow whole. When a tooth wears out or snaps, a new tooth is already growing underneath, waiting to push into the empty space.

blocks.prompt: Built to Wait
blocks.text: A crocodile looks lazy. Lying on a mudbank for six hours with its mouth hanging open is not laziness, though. It is engineering. A crocodile is an ectotherm, which means it does not burn food to make its own body heat the way you do. It borrows heat from the sun instead. When it gets too warm, it gapes its jaws and lets heat escape through the wet skin of its mouth, the way a dog pants. All of that borrowed heat is free. A person your size has to eat every single day just to stay warm. A large crocodile can go for months between meals, because it is not paying that bill. The rest of the body is built around the same idea: spend almost nothing, then spend everything at once. A crocodile can rest underwater for an hour or more. It slows its heart until it beats only a couple of times a minute and lets the oxygen it already has last and last. A muscular flap at the back of its throat seals the passage to its lungs, so it can open its jaws underwater without drowning. Scattered across its jaws are thousands of small black dots. Each one is a pressure sensor, and together they read the faintest ripple in the water. In total darkness, in water too muddy to see a hand in, a crocodile knows exactly where something touched the surface. Then comes the spending. The lunge takes less than a second, and the bite that ends it is the strongest ever measured on a living animal. Everything else in a crocodile's day is saving up for that one moment.

blocks.prompt: The Tenderness of a Killing Machine
blocks.text: Nothing alive bites harder than a crocodile. Researchers spent years persuading crocodilians to clamp down on an armored sensor, and a saltwater crocodile eventually registered about 3,700 pounds per square inch. A human manages roughly 150. That bite is the most famous fact about crocodiles, and it hides the more interesting one. The same animal is one of the most careful parents in the reptile world. Consider what most reptiles do. A sea turtle drags herself up a beach, buries a few hundred eggs, and swims away forever. The hatchlings dig themselves out and run a gauntlet alone. That is the normal reptile bargain: lay plenty, protect none, and let the numbers do the work. A mother crocodile refuses the bargain. She builds a nest, either a hole dug in sun-warmed sand or a mound of rotting plants that heats itself as it decays, and then she stays. For roughly three months she guards it, chasing off monitor lizards and anything else that comes near, sometimes going hungry rather than abandoning her post. The nest is doing quiet work in the meantime. A crocodile egg has no fixed sex when it is laid. The temperature inside the nest decides it. Middle temperatures produce mostly males, while cooler and hotter nests produce mostly females, which means the weather of a single season shapes the next generation. When the hatchlings are ready, they begin to chirp from inside their shells. The sound carries up through the sand, and the mother digs down to reach them. Then the animal with the strongest bite on Earth takes each newborn between its teeth, holds it there without leaving a scratch, and carries it to the water. She may guard those hatchlings for months more, and some mothers will answer a distress call from a baby that is not even theirs. There is one last piece of unfinished business. We say crocodile tears to mean fake sorrow, from an old story about a beast that weeps while it eats. Researchers decided to check. They watched crocodilians feed on dry land, and the eyes really did water. The tears are real, but the sorrow is not. The best explanation is plain plumbing: the huffing and hissing of a feeding crocodile pushes air through sinuses that sit beside the tear glands, and the glands empty. It is worth pausing on how strange all of this is. The bite, the babysitting, and the weeping come from the same skull. We remember the first, invented a lie about the third, and overlooked the second entirely, mostly because a monster makes a better story than a mother. The crocodile does not care which one we tell.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Crocodylus porosus: the largest living reptile
Archosaurs: crocodilians and birds are the only survivors
Four-chambered heart, like a bird's, unusual for a reptile
Integumentary sense organs read pressure waves in the dark
Temperature-dependent sex determination in every nest
It walked through the extinction that ended the dinosaurs

blocks.prompt: Living Fossil Is the Wrong Phrase
blocks.text: People like to call the crocodile a living fossil, an animal that stopped bothering to change. The phrase is comforting and wrong, and taking it apart tells you more about evolution than the compliment ever could. Start with the family tree. Crocodiles are archosaurs, members of the great ruling-reptile lineage that also produced the dinosaurs. Two branches of that group are still here. One of them is the crocodilians. The other is birds, which means a saltwater crocodile is more closely related to a sparrow than to a lizard. Sixty-six million years ago an asteroid ended the non-avian dinosaurs, and crocodilians walked through that extinction without much fuss. Small, cold-running, semi-aquatic animals that could go months without eating were exactly the wrong thing to kill by blocking out the sun. Now look at what the survivors are actually carrying. A crocodile has a four-chambered heart, the same design a bird or a mammal has, and no other reptile does. It has integumentary sense organs, thousands of pigmented domes across its jaws that detect pressure waves so faint they can locate a single drop striking the surface in total darkness. It has a palatal valve, a muscular seal at the back of the throat that lets it open its mouth underwater without flooding its lungs. True crocodiles excrete surplus salt through glands on the tongue, which is why they can cross open ocean while alligators cannot. Its teeth are replaced continually, each socket cycling through new teeth for a lifetime, so it never faces the toothless old age that finishes off an aging lion. Its nest has no fixed sex until the sand around it settles on a temperature. Even the famous jaw is a study in economy. The muscles that close it are vast, and the muscles that open it are so slight that a person can hold those jaws shut barehanded, because in millions of years of ambushing, nothing has ever needed prying off. None of that is a fossil. That is a specification list, and every item on it was selected for. So why does the shape look so old? Because the shape works. The ambush predator that lies at the boundary between land and water, invisible until it is not, has been a solvable problem for a very long time, and crocodilians solved it early. The fossil record is blunt about this. Ancient crocodile relatives were not all low, flat, patient things. Some were slender runners with long legs that chased prey overland. Some were ocean swimmers with flippers and a fish-like tail. Some were plant eaters. That whole range of experiments existed and then closed, and the branch that lasted is the one lying still in the shallows. The crocodile is not the ancestor that never changed. It is the version that kept working while its stranger cousins did not. Evolution is not a ladder climbing toward complexity. It is a fit between an animal and a world, and when the world holds still, so does the fit. The crocodile is not proof that evolution stopped. It is proof that evolution finished. There is one more reason the phrase deserves retiring. Living fossil implies an animal safely past the point of danger, a survivor of everything, needing nothing from us. But some crocodilian species are now critically endangered, and the reason is not an asteroid. It is habitat drained for farmland, hides taken for leather, and rivers dammed and poisoned. A lineage that shrugged off the death of the dinosaurs is being undone in a couple of human centuries. Calling it a fossil lets us look away from that. It survived every catastrophe the planet produced. It has not yet survived us.
